claims.text: Sharding stores each row in exactly one of several databases, usually on separate servers, chosen from a value of the row (the shard key); each shard holds only its share of the rows.
claims.source_hint: General database architecture definition; content/glossary.yaml terms sharding, database-shard, shard-key

claims.text: In PostgreSQL, % on integers returns the remainder of the division (5 % 4 = 1); for the non-negative ids of donhang_perf it yields 0-3.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 9.3 Mathematical Functions and Operators (% modulo)

claims.text: Partitions live inside one database and PostgreSQL itself skips the partitions a query cannot need (pruning at planning or execution); with shards in separate databases, the code sending a query must choose the database (connection) before sending it.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 5.12.4 Partition Pruning; 22.1 Managing Databases, Overview (a connection is to one database); prereq backend.l3.table-partitioning

claims.text: Each shard brings its own CPU, disk and connections, so write capacity grows with the number of shards as long as writes spread over them.
claims.source_hint: General scaling principle; condition stated (writes must spread evenly)

claims.text: A PostgreSQL query cannot reference tables in another database, and an ordinary (non-two-phase) transaction runs on one connection, i.e. one database; so a query or transaction reaches only one shard's rows.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 22.1 Managing Databases, Overview (a connection accesses one database; cross-database references are not supported); SQL command BEGIN

claims.text: order_items at stage-3 has no customer_id column (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_vnd), so sharding by customer_id places each item on its order's shard.

Rows usually read together should share a shard key, and among such keys prefer one where no single value holds a large share: when one customer's history is the common read, sharding orders and order_items by customer_id keeps it on one shard, readable with one JOIN.
claims.source_hint: Condition stated (when the common read is per customer); outline item 5

claims.text: With a shard key computed from a value (here value % N), every row with the same key value lands on the same shard regardless of the shard count, so one value holding a large share of rows makes a hot shard.
claims.source_hint: Follows from a deterministic key-to-shard function; shard-skew.sql comment lines 6-7

claims.text: A database per tenant is sharding with the tenant id as the shard key; a large shop can be a hot shard by itself.
At stage-3 Đơn Hàng is not sharded; shard-skew.sql only counts with GROUP BY where donhang_perf's orders would land with 4 shards, without copying or moving rows.
sum(count(*)) OVER () is a window aggregate over all result rows of the grouped query, so it equals the total count; percent = each group's share, rounded to 1 decimal by round(x, 1).
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 3.5 Window Functions; 4.2.8 Window Function Calls; 9.3 round(numeric, integer)

claims.text: donhang_perf has 20 customers and 200,000 orders; customer 1 has 81% (g % 100 < 81), each of customers 2-20 has 1% (2,000 orders).

shard-skew.sh @ stage-3: lines 6-9 run perf-db.sh --if-missing (build donhang_perf only if absent) then re-run inside a prepared container (lab-run.sh); lines 11-14 run shard-skew.sql with psql, PostgreSQL's command-line client, against host db (the compose service name).
shard-skew.sh output @ stage-3: by customer_id % 4, shards 0-3 hold 10000/170000/10000/10000 orders (5.0/85.0/5.0/5.0%); by id % 4, 50000 each (25.0%).
Shard 1 under customer_id % 4 holds customers 1, 5, 9, 13, 17: 81% + 4 x 1% = 85%; with any shard count, the shard holding customer 1 holds at least 81%.
